title: ELSSA: Explainable large language model-based decision support for public transit incident management
abstract: Rapid incident response in public transit requires supervisors to make defensible decisions that align with both formal standard operating procedures (SOPs) and practical agency experience recorded in past reports. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) often fragments handbook context and underutilizes precedent knowledge embedded in unstructured control narratives. We present ELSSA, an Experience- and Logic-integrated System for Supervisor Assistance, which unifies rule-based and experience-based evidence for explainable incident-management support. ELSSA couples (i) a hierarchy-aware RAG pipeline over a structured ontology of the Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) incident handbook, and (ii) a knowledge-graph–based RAG module that converts TTC service occurrence reports into a regularized transit-incident knowledge graph via lightweight frequency-based auto-regularization; hybrid semantic and graph retrieval then surfaces relevant clauses and structurally similar precedents. Experiments using TTC supervisor training materials and Route 29 service occurrence reports show that ELSSA improves rule-based SOP question answering over strong RAG baselines and produces more robust experience-based control suggestions across original, radio-style, and paraphrased incident descriptions. A temporally separated 2023 held-out database further provides an initial test of generalization to newly received reports. A compliance analysis shows that service recovery and core documentation elements are highly visible in historical records which reflacts the reliability of the suggestions from ELSSA. Overall, ELSSA demonstrates how hierarchy-aware SOP retrieval and regularized incident knowledge graphs can support evidence-linked, auditable, and human-supervised decision assistance for public transit operations.

title: Cross-city generalization of machine learning surrogates for road capacity reductions via transfer learning
abstract: Agent-based transport models (ABM) can model traffic policies with high fidelity, but their computational cost makes systematic exploration of large intervention spaces infeasible. Recent work shows that machine learning surrogates can approximate ABM outcomes at link level in milliseconds, enabling rapid evaluation and optimization over large intervention spaces. However, a key practical barrier remains: accurate surrogates typically require thousands of computationally expensive ABM simulations for training.This paper investigates whether that barrier can be overcome through cross-city transfer learning, and whether it is therefore meaningful to build a reusable multi-city "surrogate database" that can be efficiently fine-tuned to new target cities with minimal additional simulation effort. We propose a transferable surrogate with a hybrid Graph Neural Network - Transformer architecture, pretrained on multiple source cities and fine-tuned in a few-shot manner on a target city.Using MATSim capacity-reduction interventions across several small- and mid-sized cities, we show that few-shot fine-tuning consistently outperforms training from scratch across all target cities and target-city data budgets. Transfer performance further improves with the number and diversity of source cities, and we analyze which factors drive strong transfer. Beyond predictive accuracy, we evaluate decision-relevant performance in the intended workflow: ranking candidate interventions under an objective and feasibility constraints and validating only a small elite subset with the computationally expensive ABM. The surrogate closely reproduces the ABM’s top-ranked scenarios while being orders of magnitude faster than ABM evaluation and reduces simulation core-hour requirements by up to 99% relative to training a separate surrogate per city.

title: Reservation scheme for congestion management during morning commute: Considering noncompliance
abstract: Noncompliance --- the failure of commuters to travel within their reserved time interval --- poses a fundamental challenge to reservation-based travel demand management (TDM) schemes that rely on precise supply--demand matching. We develop an analytical framework for a reservation scheme that systematically conceptualizes and incorporates noncompliance into both scheme design and equilibrium analysis. The authority divides the morning peak into a shoulder--central--shoulder interval structure and distributes quotas accordingly; the noncompliance probability is formulated as a design-sensitive function of the time-interval structure, establishing a principled link between interval design and noncompliance behavior. Three equilibria are derived hierarchically --- the departure time equilibrium (within each interval), the rescheduling equilibrium (across intervals following noncompliance), and the long-term equilibrium (across the implementation cycle) --- and their properties are characterized analytically. Numerical analyses reveal that, while noncompliance generally exacerbates system and travel time costs, this adverse effect can be fully neutralized through appropriate time interval division, which guarantees the proposed scheme's superiority over the laissez-faire case at any noncompliance level. Counterintuitively, noncompliance improves system performance in certain extreme scenarios. Although noncompliance increases total schedule delay costs, the improvement in travel time costs fully offsets this disadvantage, confirming the scheme's overall effectiveness. We provide tailored policy design insights for two distinct managerial objectives: minimizing system cost and ensuring long-term fairness. Furthermore, the analytical insights regarding noncompliance could serve as a methodological reference for broader capacity-constrained reservation systems.

title: Evacuation behaviors of electric vehicle drivers: route and charging choice experiments
abstract: During habitual travel, electric vehicle (EV) drivers’ routes and charging infrastructure choices are associated with their vehicle’s driving range, recharging times, and infrastructure access. During an extreme event that warrants evacuation, motorists’ decisions (e.g., routing) are associated with personal and household characteristics, regional and road features, and the hazard’s severity. As the number of EV drivers increases in our road networks, vehicle technological specifications may further complicate evacuation routing and charging decisions. We conduct a stated preference (SP) survey and statistical modeling to identify the effect of electric vehicle specifications and charging station characteristics on EV drivers’ evacuation decisions: routing and charging choices. The stated preference survey consists of 12 route choice experiments of short- and long-distance evacuation simulations under mandatory evacuation orders. The survey considered key attributes, including evacuation distance, travel time, queuing and charging duration, battery state of charge, locations of charging stations, and correlation between route choices. The data was analyzed using two discrete choice models: a multinomial logit model and a two-level nested logit model. Our findings uncover the effects of vehicle and charging station characteristics on EV drivers’ evacuation behavior, while the behavioral model coupled with stochastic user equilibrium traffic assignment capture evacuation flows in the Chicago and South Florida networks, inform policy implications and provide evacuation preparedness recommendations.

title: Hybrid safe reinforcement learning for take-off and merging trajectory optimization in urban air mobility
abstract: The take-off and merging phases of electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft in structured air corridors pose highly safety-critical and computationally demanding trajectory optimization problems. These challenges arise from high-dimensional dynamics, strong vehicle coupling, and high safety requirements. This paper proposes a Hybrid Safe reinforcement learning (RL) framework to address the eVTOL take-off and merging trajectory optimization problem under complex safety constraints. To enhance safety, we employ model-based higher-order control barrier functions (HOCBFs) to encode complex safety constraints. We incorporate the differentiable HOCBF loss into the policy optimization via adaptive Lagrange multipliers to create a “gradient-based fence” that guides safety adherence during the learning process. Furthermore, to overcome the performance limitations of existing safe RL methods based on single-layer neural networks, we introduce a deep RL architecture with a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB)-guidance critic training scheme. This model-driven scheme promotes adherence to optimality conditions, leading to a stable approximation of the optimal control value and enhanced trajectory optimality. Extensive simulations are conducted under representative eVTOL take-off and merging scenarios, including operations with and without preceding merging eVTOLs as well as uncertainty-aware environments. The results demonstrate improved safety and robustness performance compared with PPO-based baselines. Furthermore, ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the HJB-guidance mechanism, while comparisons with numerical optimization methods show comparable trajectory performance with substantially improved computational efficiency. These findings indicate that the Hybrid Safe RL algorithm has the potential for real-time and safety-enhanced deployment in future corridor-based take-off and merging operations of eVTOLs.

title: Dial-a-ride problem with goods delivery using drones
abstract: Online ordering and delivery of products has grown significantly in recent years. In addition, the transport of people from a desired origin to a desired destination has become increasingly important. We present a novel mathematical model that aims to combine the transport of products by drones with the transport of dial-a-ride customers by people carriers. This novel approach is called the dial-a-ride problem with drones, or DARPD for short. In the DARPD, passenger vehicles that transport dial-a-ride customers are equipped with drones, allowing them to deliver parcels to recipients simultaneously with the passenger transport. The DARPD determines the route for the passenger transport and enables the drone to take off from the desired locations and destinations of the dial-a-ride customers. A drone can independently deliver products to one or more parcel customers. After delivery, the drone returns to the dial-a-ride transport vehicle, where its battery is replaced to make it fully operational again. The strength of this novel concept is demonstrated through a computational study. The results show that combining passenger transport with parallel product delivery by drones can yield significant economic and ecological benefits.

title: Synchronous truck-robot-drone last-mile delivery
abstract: The continued growth of online shopping in recent years has placed greater demands on efficient last-mile delivery systems. Traditional truck parcel delivery faces challenges such as slow delivery in congested urban areas and high environmental impacts. These issues have inspired researchers and practitioners to develop novel multi-modal delivery systems based on the coordination between traditional delivery trucks and newer technologies such as delivery robots and drones. In this paper, we model a synchronous truck-robot-drone last-mile delivery system and propose a mixed integer program along with a heuristic solution. The proposed model is designed for a delivery truck equipped with a multi-visit drone and multiple single-delivery robots. The model accounts for multiple operational constraints, including drone energy endurance and the load capacities of both the drone and the robots. Computational experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed heuristic in solving real-sized instances. The impact of the proposed delivery system is evaluated using the 2021 Amazon Last Mile Routing Research Challenge dataset in Seattle. The case results show that replacing the truck with the proposed system can reduce travel times within customer zones by an average of 40% compared to the original routes. Time savings can reach up to 52% for larger deliveries, demonstrating the system’s potential to improve efficiency and contribute to reduced environmental impacts in urban logistics.

title: Uncertainty quantification for traffic state estimation at signalized intersections with low penetration vehicle trajectory data
abstract: This study investigates the problem of traffic state estimation at signalized intersections using low-penetration-rate vehicle trajectory data. While prior research has proposed various methods to estimate unknown traffic states and parameters—such as queue length and penetration rate—most provide only point estimates and do not characterize the uncertainty arising from sparse and noisy observations. However, understanding this uncertainty is essential for assessing the reliability of estimation results and for determining whether the available data are sufficient to support operational decision-making. To address this limitation, we develop a Bayesian estimation framework that yields distributional outputs, explicitly quantifying estimation uncertainty. The framework is built upon a novel hidden Markov model (HMM) formulation, in which a point-queue process captures the latent traffic dynamics, and an observation model connects the observed trajectories with the unknown quantities to be estimated. We also derive a recursive algorithm to estimate the unknown traffic states and parameters simultaneously. The proposed method is evaluated through simulation, and a comprehensive sensitivity analysis is conducted to examine how key factors influence the accuracy and uncertainty of the estimation results.

title: Analysis of ride-hailing systems’ stability and dynamics around equilibrium points
abstract: Emerging transportation services, particularly ride-hailing, are rapidly reshaping urban mobility and often outpacing our understanding of their operational characteristics. A prominent challenge in these services is the ``wild goose chase" (WGC) phenomenon, an inefficient state resulting from dynamic and stochastic behavior. Despite its prominence, no systematic and rigorous framework currently exists to assess its effects over the stability of the system equilibrium points or predict its duration. Herein, this study proposes such a framework to assess the stability of equilibrium points, and provide accurate predictions on the duration of the WGC phenomenon. The main findings used pivotal operational thresholds (e.g., equilibrium points and the boundary between efficient and inefficient operational conditions) to identify three regions with contrasting efficiency and stability characteristics. A queuing model is developed and compared to a numerical simulation, demonstrating that the efficient equilibrium is not the most typical operating state unless fleet sizes significantly exceed a determined minimum threshold. Moreover, the queuing model quantifies the risks associated with prolonged operation in inefficient states, revealing potential system instability. These results reveal previously overlooked risks for ride-hailing services associated with long and repeated periods of inefficient operation. By enabling quantitative characterization of the WGC phenomenon, this work offers a fundamental tool for guiding future research and informing operational strategies in ride-hailing services.

title: Multimodal multiscale signal-vehicle coupled control
abstract: New advancements enabled by the connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) have made possible the effective cooperation between road users and traffic infrastructure towards more sustainable, efficient and safe mobility in transportation networks. This study extends a Signal-Vehicle Coupled Control (SVCC) model to optimize traffic signals and CAV trajectories at intersections for various transportation modes, including active transportation (Pedestrians and Cyclists) and vehicles with different power sources (e.g., fuel, hybrid and electric) and CAVs. An optimization framework is developed using a Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme with the objective of minimizing vehicle, pedestrians and cyclists’ delay as well as minimizing the fuel and energy consumption of vehicles at the intersection. The framework is capable of coordinating CAVs and signal controllers under various infrastructure configurations. These include concurrent and exclusive pedestrian and bicycle phasing, various vehicle turning treatments, as well as mixed and separated bike flows. The results demonstrate that integrating pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicle heterogeneity into the optimization process through the proposed Multimodal Multiscale SVCC (M2SVCC) yields superior performance compared to conventional actuated signal control. Specifically, M2SVCC achieves significant reductions in fuel and energy consumption (sustainability), user delays (mobility), and traffic conflicts (safety) across a range of active user demands and signal configurations.
